title: Task-Directed Spectral Design for Local Quantum Tomography
abstract: Many tomography tasks require only a low-dimensional function of the state. We study local pure-state tomography under projective-fidelity access when a parametric model, a credible center, and a differentiable downstream task are known before acquisition. The pullback Fubini--Study metric and the task metric define coordinate-invariant generalized eigendirections, which we realize as a fixed library of geodesic fidelity probes. We prove two optimality results: the probe aligned with a task coordinate is its unique variance-minimizing location up to orientation, and, when prior and measurement information are diagonal in this basis, a diminishing-return greedy rule exactly minimizes the integer-budget local task-variance surrogate over the spectral library. Under common per-shot information and the stated large-budget condition, the absolute and relative gaps to arbitrary probe directions are respectively \(O(B^{-3})\) and \(O(B^{-2})\). A closed-form local estimator is followed by a task-metric localization projection that cannot increase quadratic task loss when localization holds. In six-qubit numerical experiments, the Schmidt-spectrum design activates only one or two settings and has lower mean task error than the post hoc best adaptive results across all tested dimensions and copy budgets. For full-state tomography, it likewise has lower mean infidelity throughout the tested local regime. The fixed batch uses no feedback loops and far fewer settings; under the illustrative latency model, its acquisition cost is roughly three to four orders of magnitude lower than that of the adaptive methods.
summary: This work proposes a novel, fixed-batch protocol for local quantum tomography that targets only the necessary information for a specific task. By optimizing measurement probes based on a combination of geometric fidelity and task sensitivity, the method achieves state-of-the-art performance with significantly lower experimental overhead than adaptive techniques. This advances the practical feasibility of quantum state characterization in resource-constrained quantum computing settings.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of performing quantum tomography by estimating only a low-dimensional function of the quantum state, rather than the full state, to improve efficiency.
main_result: A fixed-batch, task-directed measurement design was shown to achieve lower mean task error and significantly lower acquisition cost compared to adaptive methods in numerical experiments.
method: The authors derive optimal measurement directions using a generalized eigenproblem involving the pullback Fubini-Study metric and a task-specific metric, leading to a fixed, non-adaptive probe library.
model_or_system: The study focuses on pure-state quantum systems parameterized by a differentiable model on a projective Hilbert space, analyzed using local coordinates.
key_observables: Mean task error, mean infidelity, task loss, and acquisition cost ratios.
important_parameters: The measurement budget ($B$), the localization radius ($R$), and the dimensionality of the system ($d$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a known parametric model, a credible center, and relies on the large-budget condition and the localization assumption.
figures_summary: Tables compare task MSE and full-state infidelity across various dimensions, budgets, and measurement strategies, showing the fixed spectral design outperforms adaptive methods.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the geometric constraints (local invariance, localization radius) to formulating a Bayesian optimization problem, which is then approximated locally using Fisher information to determine the optimal fixed probe set and shot allocation.
why_interesting: The development of fixed, non-adaptive protocols that outperform adaptive ones is crucial for scaling quantum experiments, especially when feedback loops are costly or impossible to implement.
